newsitem.title: USA: US stocks seen higher at open, completing rebound.
newsitem.headline: US stocks seen higher at open, completing rebound.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open higher, completing a rebound from early Friday, when investors sold heavily after cautionary market-related comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Analysts said markets would likely draw confidence from the fact that by the end of Friday's session, most of the selling damage to U.S. shares had already been undone.
"It looks like it's a recovery morning," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "Friday afternoon we were recovering and that carried over to Europe."

"I don't think the market's going to be as exuberant," Wachtel said, alluding to Greenspan's rhetorical question regarding "irrational exuberance" in the market. "There's going to be a sense someone's watching but nothing fundamental has changed."

While the momentary shock wave from Greenspan's speech seems to have passed, analysts cautioned that more selling could be in store for the Dow industrials, which were in the midst of a pullback even before Friday's session.
"We're still in a corrective stage," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"I suspect we're going to have a rebound at the open but perhaps some selling will develop late," Cardillo said. "We've gotten two percent (lower) and we'll probably have some more."
Markets will not have any significant economic data to contend with today, but the semiconductor industry's monthly book-to-bill report is expected after the session's close.
Chip makers Intel Corp and Texas Instruments Inc were among U.S. shares trading slightly firmer in London. The FTSE-100 climbed 31.6 points to 3994.6.
In Tokyo, stocks staged a strong rally after posting their largest one-day selloff of the year last Friday.
The Nikkei-225 index surged 327 points to 20,604.
The dollar was little changed in Tokyo, holding a whisker below 113 yen, and wended higher at just above 1.55 marks in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were firmer, with the benchmark 30-year bond up 12 ticks to yield 6.48 percent.
The December S&P 500 index gained three points to 743.50.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column focuses on some mutual fund sales of junk bonds in Marvel Entertainment Group Inc, which took place just prior to the announcement of unfavorable developments at the company.
